aiOverview.content: Measles is a highly contagious viral respiratory disease that causes a high fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes, and a characteristic blotchy rash. It is caused by the measles virus and spreads through air or direct contact with an infected person. Vaccination is the best prevention; there is no specific antiviral treatment, though supportive care and vitamin A are recommended. Symptoms Initial: High fever, cough, runny nose, and red/watery eyes (conjunctivitis). Early Signs: Small white spots (Koplik spots) may appear inside the cheeks. Rash: A red, blotchy rash appears 3-5 days after initial symptoms, starting on the face/neck and spreading downward, lasting 5-6 days. Timing: Symptoms usually appear 7–14 days after exposure. Causes and Transmission Cause: Measles virus (rubeola). Transmission: Highly contagious, spreading through coughing, sneezing, and close contact. Environmental Stability: The virus can live in the air or on surfaces for up to two hours. Contagious Period: Infected individuals can spread the virus from 4 days before the rash appears until 4 days after. ComplicationsMeasles can lead to severe health issues, particularly in children under 5 and adults over 20. Common: Ear infections and severe diarrhea. Serious: Pneumonia (most common cause of death), severe breathing problems, and encephalitis (brain swelling). Long-term: Blindness, or in rare cases, permanent brain damage. Pregnancy: Increased risk of miscarriage, premature birth, or low birth weight. Treatment and Prevention Vaccination: The MMR (measles, mumps, and rubella) vaccine is safe and highly effective. Two doses are 97% effective. Treatment: No specific antiviral treatment exists. Treatment involves supportive care: rest, fluids, fever reduction, and vitamin A for children. Prevention: Vaccination is the primary prevention method. Recent Data (2026)As of March 19, 2026, the United States has experienced high cases, with 1,487 confirmed, largely driven by outbreaks, confirming the high transmissibility of the virus among unvaccinated individuals CDC (2026 data).
